notes: Confidential trade secrets trial; public judgment dismisses EPI claims except nominal damages.

enrichment.short_title: EPI v Symphony: degradable plastic additive confidentiality and passing off
key_facts: EPI alleged Symphony copied its confidential degradable plastic additive formulation DCP 509 in creating BD92384 for thin-film products such as carrier bags.
The dispute arose under confidentiality agreements between the parties and included a passing-off claim.
The trial was conducted in private under a confidentiality club because of sensitive formulation evidence.
EPI sought relief for breach of confidentiality clauses and misuse of confidential information.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery trial of claims for breach of confidence, contractual confidentiality and passing off, with a split public judgment.
enrichment.outcome: EPI's claims were dismissed except for breach of clause 14.8 and entitlement to nominal damages for breach of clause 14.4.
enrichment.ratio: Where confidential formulation evidence is disputed, the court must assess witness credibility rigorously, including expert evidence tested in cross-examination; a witness may lie without destroying an otherwise good case, but failure to challenge opposing points at trial may disentitle a party from relying on them at closing.
legal_issues: Whether Symphony's BD92384 formulation was a substantial copy of EPI's confidential DCP 509
Whether Symphony breached confidentiality agreements and misused confidential information
Whether Symphony passed off its products as associated with EPI
How credibility and expert evidence should be evaluated at trial
linked_authorities: Phillips & Others v Symes & Others [2004] EWHC 2330 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Public judgment clearly states dismissal and nominal damages; confidential findings are in a separate non-public part.

notes: Section 17 succession appeal; Recorder's permanence test upheld on homosexual partner facts.

enrichment.short_title: Nutting v SHG: assured tenancy succession and same-sex partner permanence
key_facts: Mark Nutting lived with assured tenant Mr Roberts in a volatile same-sex relationship for just over two years before Roberts died.
Southern Housing Group sought possession of flat 6, contending Nutting did not succeed under section 17 as Roberts' spouse or treated spouse.
The relationship was tempestuous, involved heavy drinking and was not consistently presented as permanent to outsiders.
The Recorder held Nutting failed to show sufficient commitment to permanence for succession.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Chancery Division from a possession trial deciding section 17 Housing Act 1988 succession.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Nutting was not entitled to succeed to the assured tenancy.
enrichment.ratio: For section 17(4) succession a person living with the tenant as wife or husband must show a relationship openly and unequivocally displayed with sufficient commitment to permanence akin to marriage; cohabitation and mutual support alone are insufficient without lifetime commitment.
legal_issues: Whether Nutting was treated as the tenant's spouse under section 17(4)
What test applies to permanence in same-sex succession cases after Ghaidan v Mendoza
Whether the Recorder's factual findings on commitment to permanence were open to him
Whether possession should follow failure of succession
linked_authorities: Fitzpatrick v Sterling Housing Association Ltd [1999] 4 All ER 705

confidence.notes: Statutory test, factual findings and appellate disposition are all clearly reasoned.

notes: Construction adjudication enforcement; Serco could not withhold liquidated damages against adjudicator's sum.

enrichment.short_title: Balfour Beatty v Serco: summary enforcement of motorway VMS adjudication award

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Serco engaged Balfour Beatty under a 2001 contract to design, supply and install 104 motorway variable message signs.
A dispute over extensions of time and liquidated damages was referred to adjudication.
The adjudicator awarded Balfour Beatty a substantial sum; Serco refused payment and sought to set off liquidated damages.
Balfour Beatty applied for summary judgment to enforce the adjudicator's decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court application for summary judgment enforcing an adjudicator's award.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted; Balfour Beatty was entitled to enforce the adjudicator's award without set-off of liquidated damages, with remaining merits issues left for later resolution.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator's decision on a referred dispute is temporarily binding and enforceable by summary judgment; a paying party may not withhold the adjudicator's sum by set-off of a separate liquidated damages claim absent effective withholding notices under section 111.
legal_issues: What Balfour Beatty was entitled to recover under the adjudicator's decision
Whether Serco could set off liquidated and ascertained damages against the adjudicator's sum
Whether Serco's correspondence constituted effective section 111 withholding notices
Whether summary enforcement should be stayed pending final determination

notes: Leading ground 8 housing benefit adjournment authority; four consolidated possession appeals dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Housing benefit arrears: adjournment and mandatory ground 8 possession
key_facts: Four assured tenants of housing associations fell more than eight weeks into rent arrears through housing benefit maladministration or processing delays.
Possession proceedings were brought on mandatory ground 8; each tenant sought adjournment to pay off arrears.
District judges refused adjournments, holding they lacked jurisdiction or that adjournment would undermine section 7(3).
The cases illustrated widespread problems when reclaim forms were lost and benefit offices could not rectify arrears before hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated Court of Appeal appeals from mandatory ground 8 possession orders in county court rent arrears cases.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; district judges were right to refuse adjournments in these cases.
enrichment.ratio: Where ground 8 is established the court must make a possession order once satisfied the landlord is entitled; adjourning solely so a tenant can reduce arrears below the eight-week threshold defeats the statutory scheme and is permissible only in exceptional circumstances, not merely because housing benefit was wrongly withheld.
legal_issues: Whether the court may adjourn ground 8 possession claims to allow tenants to pay arrears
Whether housing benefit maladministration constitutes exceptional circumstances
Construction of sections 7, 8 and 9 of the Housing Act 1988
When the court becomes satisfied for section 9(6) purposes
linked_authorities: R v Walsall Justices, ex parte W (a minor) [1990] 1 QB 253
Bristol City Council v Lovell [1998] 1 WLR 446
Kingcastle Ltd v Owen Owen (Court of Appeal, 19 February 1999)

confidence.notes: Authoritative multi-case analysis with explicit holding on adjournment power and final order.

notes: Section 65 young offender supervision licence; Article 5 challenge to hostel conditions dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Davies: judicial review of probation hostel residence and escort licence terms
key_facts: Owen Davies was released from a young offender institution after serving 30 months for deception, burglary and aggravated vehicle taking offences.
A section 65 supervision notice required permanent residence at Lawson House probation hostel and rarely imposed escorted-leave conditions.
Davies challenged the hostel residence and escort requirements as an unlawful Article 5 deprivation of liberty.
The supervision period was three months and the escort condition was subject to monthly review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court judicial review, with permission, of licence conditions on release under section 65 of the 1991 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the cumulative licence restrictions did not amount to a deprivation of liberty under Article 5.
enrichment.ratio: Mandatory probation hostel residence combined with a temporary escort requirement for a three-month section 65 supervision period does not cross the Article 5 threshold where the restrictions pursue public protection and reintegration and do not constitute confinement equivalent to imprisonment.
legal_issues: Whether section 65 licence conditions requiring hostel residence were lawful
Whether the escort requirement cumulatively deprived Davies of liberty under Article 5
Whether the Secretary of State could impose rarely used escort conditions
Appropriate standard of review for release licence terms

confidence.notes: Article 5 analysis and unanimous dismissal are clearly recorded.

notes: Professional burglary gang appeal; Terry conviction dismissed, both sentences reduced to eight years.

enrichment.short_title: Colman and Terry: double jeopardy, acquittal evidence and burglary sentences
key_facts: Colman and Terry were convicted of a series of commercial burglaries and handling computer equipment stolen from warehouses in 2000.
Covert recordings from a listening device in a Fiat Punto were central prosecution evidence.
Terry appealed conviction on whether prior acquittals and excluded recordings could be used at trial; both appealed ten-year sentences.
Nine other counts were not pursued after the judge excluded expert evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeals against conviction (Terry) and sentence (both appellants).
enrichment.outcome: Terry's conviction appeal dismissed; both sentence appeals allowed in part, substituting six years for aggravated burglary and two years consecutive for handling, reducing total custody from ten to eight years.
enrichment.ratio: An acquittal is conclusive between the parties on the charge acquitted but does not automatically exclude all related evidence at a separate trial; however consecutive sentences must reflect the overall criminality, and treating handling as wholly separate from the same course of conduct can produce a disproportionate total.
legal_issues: Admissibility and use of evidence relating to charges on which the accused was acquitted
Application of Sambasivam and the rule against double jeopardy
Whether Terry's trial was unfair because acquittals were not fully before the jury
Whether consecutive sentences for burglary and handling were manifestly excessive
linked_authorities: Sambasivam v Public Prosecutor, Federation of Malaya [1950] AC 458
R v Hay (1983) 77 Cr App R 70

confidence.notes: Conviction and sentence dispositions and Sambasivam reasoning are explicit.

notes: Landmark sports violence appeal; unsafe conviction for s20 GBH in amateur football tackle.

enrichment.short_title: R v Barnes: criminal liability for reckless tackle in amateur football
key_facts: Mark Barnes was convicted by majority verdict of section 20 GBH after a sliding tackle in an amateur football match broke Christopher Bygraves' leg.
The prosecution alleged the tackle was late, unnecessary, reckless and high; Barnes said it was a hard but fair challenge for the ball.
The jury asked for further directions after retiring but received inadequate guidance.
Barnes was sentenced to a 240-hour community punishment order and compensation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal against conviction by leave of the full court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe and the sentence and compensation order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Criminal proceedings for on-field sporting injuries should be rare where sports disciplinary processes suffice; the jury must be directed to determine what happened at the critical moment, whether the prosecution account is proved, and whether conduct fell outside what could be anticipated as legitimate sport even if the tackle might be a foul or warrant sending off.
legal_issues: When sporting conduct crosses the threshold from foul play to criminal section 20 liability
Whether the summing-up adequately explained legitimate sport and the prosecution burden
Whether a sending-off tackle can still be criminal
Whether the jury's further direction request was properly answered

confidence.notes: Appellate guidance on sports prosecutions and explicit unsafe conviction finding.

notes: FSA section 382 enforcement of PIA ombudsman pension miss-selling awards; top-up compensation ordered.

enrichment.short_title: FSA v Matthews: section 382 compensation for unpaid pension ombudsman awards
key_facts: The Matthews partnership, Williams Life Pension Mortgage and Insurance Services, advised two clients to transfer out of the Mineworkers Pension Scheme into personal pensions.
PIA Ombudsman awards in 2000 required redress for pension miss-selling but the partnership did not comply, citing insurer refusal of indemnity.
The FSA applied under section 382 for a compensation order for Merriman and Bayliss after regulatory enforcement.
The parties disputed whether compensation should be calculated on reinstatement or top-up basis.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery application by the FSA under section 382 FSMA 2000 for compensation enforcement.
enrichment.outcome: The FSA succeeded; contravention of a relevant requirement was established and compensation was ordered on a top-up basis of £52,472.23 and £29,876.97 plus £11,500 costs, with payment time agreed to 24 January 2005.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to comply with binding PIA Ombudsman awards constitutes contravention of a relevant requirement enforceable under section 382; where reinstatement would be disproportionate, just compensation may be awarded on a top-up basis using available partnership assets.
legal_issues: Whether non-compliance with PIA Ombudsman awards is a relevant requirement under section 382
Whether the awards remained binding despite Article 6 challenges
Reinstatement versus top-up calculation of pension redress
Quantum of compensation and costs against unrepresented defendants

confidence.notes: Final compensation figures, basis of award and enforcement reasoning are clearly stated.

notes: Covent Garden Market Act consent challenge; Secretary of State consent quashed on franchise construction.

enrichment.short_title: Corporation of London v SoS: Covent Garden fish and meat trading consent
key_facts: The Secretary of State consented under section 18(1)(f) to CGMA granting leases at Nine Elms for face-to-face fish and meat trading on surplus land.
The Corporation of London sought judicial review, arguing the consent unlawfully extended CGMA's horticultural market franchise.
CGMA intended to extend existing tenants' leases to permit meat and fish retail trading.
Billingsgate and Smithfield held historic monopoly market rights for fish and meat.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal with permission to apply for judicial review of the Secretary of State's May 2003 consent.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Secretary of State's consent was quashed and CGMA had no power to grant the contemplated leases.
enrichment.ratio: A market franchise for specified commodities does not entitle the grantee, even with ministerial consent under section 18(1)(f), to authorise trading in other commodities; local personal Acts benefiting the market authority should be construed strictly against the beneficiary.
legal_issues: Construction of section 18(1)(f) second limb consent power
Whether CGMA could authorise fish and meat trading at Nine Elms
Impact on Billingsgate and Smithfield market rights
Whether disturbance of other London markets could be decided on judicial review

confidence.notes: Statutory construction, quashing order and franchise analysis are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: GMC PPC referral challenge over withdrawal of treatment; all judicial review grounds dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: David v GMC: referral to PCC after withdrawal of intensive care treatment
key_facts: Dr David, a consultant anaesthetist, withdrew intensive care from patient Robert Symons who died at Basildon Hospital in February 1999.
After police and CPS declined prosecution, the GMC reconsidered the case following new expert reports from Mrs Symons' clinical negligence claim.
The PPC referred the case to the Professional Conduct Committee for inquiry into serious professional misconduct.
Dr David challenged the referral as an improper reopening and argued the PPC misapplied the filtering test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of a GMC Preliminary Proceedings Committee decision to refer a doctor to the Professional Conduct Committee.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the PPC lawfully referred the case and properly considered the expert material before it.
enrichment.ratio: New expert medical reports may constitute fresh information under rule 14 permitting PPC reconsideration where no full PCC inquiry has occurred; where there is a real prospect that serious professional misconduct may be established, referral to the PCC is mandatory even where ethical issues in end-of-life care are involved.
legal_issues: Whether the PPC could reopen the Symons case after earlier non-referral
Whether an expert report counts as new information under rule 14
Whether ethical end-of-life issues preclude GMC disciplinary referral
Whether the PPC failed to take account of Dr Coates' report

confidence.notes: Multiple grounds addressed with clear dismissal; some factual complexity on expert evidence conflict.
